In France, demonstrations over the rising cost of living turned violent yesterday,
as protesters destroyed property and charred streets and buildings in cities across the country.
And Fierce Eleanor Beardsley has more.
There was wide-scale looting, but other cultural heritage losses were even more devastating.
A 140-year-old town hall was largely destroyed in the central town of Limoges after mass perpetrators set the building alight.
Some 550,000 people took part in the nationwide protests that initially began with students protesting the state of education.
They now include workers angry about the cost of living, inequalities, and a government they hate.
The violence ignited due to several reasons.
Far left troublemakers looking to fight with police, outside youths who showed up to loot after stores were broken into,
and weeks of overly aggressive police tactics that have left many young protesters angry and on edge.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he's investigating the sudden speed restrictions on Kyiv's use of star shield,
the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that's used for drone operations and communications.
Zelensky says the restrictions apply only to Ukraine, not European countries, and it's not clear who's responsible.
Last week, a bipartisan group of senators called for an investigation into whether the Trump administration or its contractors had anything to do with it.
And SpaceX owner Elon Musk says the U.S. government owns and controls the system,
but Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. is not responsible.
No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn't use it.
But my understanding is it's back up and running. That's what we heard two days ago.
Zelensky says the service is still throttled.
This is Ukraine attacked Russia with dozens of drones overnight, hitting an oil terminal and another data center.
Two people were killed, including a child 11 others injured when a person drove a truck through a crowd of people at a youth sports complex in Wichita, Kansas.
Roger Noemmer from member station KMUW has more.
Police say they are still trying to piece together why a woman with two kids in her truck allegedly drove through a field where children were playing soccer.
Wichita City Councilmember Becky Tuttle says she feels for the families and onlookers.
My heart breaks not only for the people that were personally impacted, but anybody who maybe observed the horrible tragedy that happened today.
Wichita Police Captain Aaron Moses says the driver of the truck is in custody and cooperating with authorities.
We have a really good idea of what happened. What we're working to do now is do the investigation to determine how it happened and why.
Officials are asking anyone with video or photos from the incident to share them with police.
For NPR News, I'm Roger Noemmer in Wichita.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
In Canada, officials say an incident at a military base in Alberta causing a major fire has left people dead and injured.
Firefighters worked late into the night battling the blaze as fierce winds whipped up the flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding area.
It's not clear how many people were killed or injured. The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, says on social media the fire was significant and tragic, affecting military personnel.
Prime Minister Mark Carney calls it a serious incident and there's no word on a cause.
It comes as the oil-rich province holds a vote tomorrow on succeeding from Canada.
Congo says the Obela outbreak has spread to an eighth province. This says Kenya has announced four new cases. Michael Koloki has more.
In a statement yesterday, Kenyan authorities said that all four patients were already in quarantine when they developed symptoms, adding that tests confirmed they have the Bundebugia strain of Ebola.
The statement noted that one of the four is a close male relative of the first Ebola patient in the country, who passed away earlier this month after travelling from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Kenya through Uganda.
Health officials said that the additional three new cases are health workers, who had attended to the first Ebola patient, with authorities noting that the three are receiving supportive care at a designated facility.
For NPR News, I'm Michael Koloki in Nairobi.
NPR has lost one of its own, Noah Adams, an ATC host for nearly two decades, has died. He was 84 years old. I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.
